templates.title: Make a smart inbox
templates.description: Claude reads every unread email and sorts it. You clear the pile in one pass instead of one message at a time.
templates.what_it_is:
A Gmail inbox digest and one-click triage app. It turns a noisy Gmail inbox
into a scannable digest grouped by what actually needs doing — reply-needed,
decisions pending, what you're waiting on, cold outreach + event invites,
newsletters/reading, in-product notifications, and pure noise — rendered as a
web tab you open like any other page. The problem it solves is inbox overload:
instead of scrolling a flat list, you see each message sorted into an
actionable bucket with a one-line, human-readable summary, and you clear each
item in a single click — archive, mark spam, unsubscribe (via the message's
`List-Unsubscribe` header), or mute (a self-managed Gmail label). There are two
parts. The `email-digest` skill does the thinking: it pulls recent Gmail,
classifies every message into the 10-bucket taxonomy using Gmail's own category
labels plus content-aware rules (and an optional LLM self-review pass), and
writes the result to a digest data file. The `email-review` web service reads
that file and renders the triage UI, performing the one-click Gmail actions
directly against the Gmail API. When it's running, the user opens a tab, scans
their inbox by category, expands any message to read it (rendered as real HTML,
with tracking pixels stripped), and clears the buckets — with an undo toast on
every action.
templates.author: kanjun

templates.title: Score your own work before shipping
templates.description: Four scorecards -- product, design, marketing, engineering -- that give the same answer twice.
templates.what_it_is:
Four rubrics for reviewing what you built -- product, design, marketing, engineering -- and a renderer that makes the scores reproducible

Self-review is usually worthless: it stops at the first defect it finds and
then congratulates itself. This template fixes that with four written rubrics --
product, design, marketing, engineering -- that force a review to keep going
after the obvious problems are fixed, and to score the criterion you would
rather skip. You score what you built against a rubric, fix what falls short,
re-score, and the result renders into a document anyone can check: a Markdown
file and a standalone HTML page per rubric and per review, with a
scores-at-a-glance table, a marks table per criterion, and a section per
finding. There is no service to run and no tab to open -- the output is files
on disk, generated by one command. What makes it more than a checklist is that
the totals are computed from the individual marks rather than typed, so a
review's arithmetic cannot quietly lie, and re-running the renderer reproduces
the published documents byte for byte.
templates.author: boweiliu

choices.summary: the bundled sample review is of someone else's product
choices.resolution: delete reviews/shared-apps.toml, re-run render_review.py render, and commit the emptied docs/ before writing your own review

choices.summary: the rubrics assume a browser-based product with a landing page and an email
choices.resolution: rewrite the design and marketing criteria for whatever the adopter actually ships (a CLI, a library, a service) rather than scoring irrelevant ones -- they are a starting point, not a standard

choices.summary: evidence cited by a review may contain private data
choices.resolution: decide what is publishable before citing it; screenshots of a real product routinely carry account names, hostnames, and other people's data

templates.title: Find something to do this weekend
templates.description: Kid-friendly events near home, with drive times and a warning when tickets are needed. Refreshed weekly.
templates.what_it_is:
A weekly, self-updating radar of fun, kid-appropriate local events near home -- weekend-first with drive times, source links, flags for ticketed events, and a guided setup to point it at your own city.

Family Weekend Radar solves a specific parenting problem: the best local kids'
events -- a fire-truck open house, a free museum day, a neighborhood festival --
spread by word of mouth through a network of other parents, and if you do not
have that network you simply miss them. This template stands in for that
network. Once a week it pulls a dozen Bay Area family-event sources, keeps only
the events that fit a child's age and sit within a drivable radius of home,
works out the drive time to each, de-dupes across sources, flags the caveats
(ticketed, fundraiser, registration required, unverified time), and buckets
everything into upcoming weekends plus a Thursday/Friday early-evening slot. The
result is written to a stable snapshot file.

What the user sees is a single web tab -- the "Family Weekend Radar" -- that
reads that snapshot. It opens on this weekend as a wall of cheerful event cards,
each with a colored map-pin badge showing the drive time (green for close, warm
for far), the venue and city, a one-line "why a kid would like this", caveat
badges, and a deep link to the event's own page. A pager steps forward through
the next several weekends so a parent can plan ahead, a "Meh" control
de-emphasizes things they are not interested in, and a "worth a peek yourself"
panel lists the human-only sources (parent Facebook groups, Instagram accounts)
that can't be automated. The page never fetches on load; it just renders the
latest snapshot, and shows a friendly empty state until the first weekly run has
happened.
templates.author: matthewboulos

choices.summary: the default home is a neutral San Francisco, CA city-center point
choices.resolution: set it to the adopter's real home address and coordinates via --home-address / --home-coords or the defaults in scripts/radar_config.py

choices.summary: age filter (4-7) and drive radius (60 min) are defaults
choices.resolution: adjust --age-min / --age-max and --drive-radius-min (or the config defaults) to the adopter's kids and area

choices.summary: the shipped source list in assets/sources.toml is SF Bay Area specific
choices.resolution: Bay Area adopters keep it as-is; adopters elsewhere rebuild it for their metro following the skill's 'Setting up for your area' guide, using verify-source to vet ~5-8 candidates, and swap the check-yourself panel entries

choices.summary: no weekly schedule ships with the template
choices.resolution: schedule the pipeline's 'run all' on a cadence (e.g. Monday morning) via the manage-scheduled-tasks skill

choices.summary: the web view's 'Meh' de-emphasize control is client-side only
choices.resolution: to persist preferences across weekly runs, wire the control to the pipeline's preference_profile.json

templates.title: Order the team's lunch every week
templates.description: Reads your Notion lunch page, picks options that fit everyone, and DMs the 8am reminder on Slack.
templates.what_it_is:
A weekly cycle that reads a team Notion lunch page, recommends nutrition-spec-matching options for each weekday, writes the chosen picks back to the doc, and DMs an 8am portion reminder each weekday over Slack.

This template turns "what should I eat for lunch this week?" into a short,
repeatable ritual. Each week it reads a team Notion "Lunch" page listing the
restaurants offered on each weekday, and for every day it proposes two or three
complete, balanced lunch options -- each a single, definite, verified-real dish
that meets a nutrition spec you configure (calorie band, lean-protein floor,
saturated-fat ceiling, a plate ratio, and so on), with estimated macros. It
presents the whole week to you in chat and waits for your picks. Once you choose,
it writes the order onto your line in the Notion doc (the order spec only) and
schedules a one-shot 8am reminder for each chosen weekday that DMs you that day's
dish plus any portion guidance over Slack -- then removes itself. It can run
automatically on Sunday evenings via the weekly-lunch cron automation, or on
demand any time. You supply your own nutrition targets and operating rules
through preference notes; the template ships generalized examples to start from.
templates.author: matthewboulos

choices.summary: The Notion lunch-page URL is a placeholder (<YOUR_NOTION_LUNCH_PAGE_URL> in SKILL.md).
choices.resolution: Point it at the team's own Notion 'Lunch' page: weekly toggles with a per-weekday restaurant list and a checkbox list of names.

choices.summary: The Slack DM channel id is a placeholder.
choices.resolution: Supply your own DM channel id (a D... id) via LUNCH_SLACK_CHANNEL or the fallback in send_lunch_reminder.sh; find it with conversations.open on your own Slack user id.

choices.summary: The nutrition targets and operating rules are not shipped as live config.
choices.resolution: Create private preference notes under data/memories/ from the shipped example-preferences/ and edit them to your own goals, including whose line the orders go on in Notion.

choices.summary: The reminder cron times are written in local container time with no UTC conversion.
choices.resolution: Set the container clock to your own timezone, or the 8am reminders fire at the wrong hour.

choices.summary: This Slack token type cannot use Slack's native chat.scheduleMessage.
choices.resolution: Reminders are delivered through one-shot cron entries instead; an adopter on a token that supports scheduling could simplify this, but the cron path works as shipped.

templates.title: Comment in the margin of any file
templates.description: Google-Docs-style notes on anything you write. Your agent gets pinged and answers in the thread.
templates.what_it_is:
Spec Workbench turns any plain markdown file into a living, collaboratively
annotated document -- the Google-Docs commenting model (comment, thread,
reply, resolve, suggest) applied to files that live in your git repo. You open
a document in a web view, select a phrase or a block, and leave a margin
comment; you and your agent then work the document together through threads
anchored to the exact text they are about. The twist is that every comment,
reply, suggestion, and status is written *back into the markdown file itself*
as ordinary blockquotes -- there is no database, so the file stays readable,
diffable, and versioned in git, and it degrades gracefully in any plain
markdown renderer. When you are ready for your agent to act, one "notify agent"
button stamps the document and pings the agent to sweep it. What you see when
it is running is a two-column reading view: your prose on the left, the live
thread margin on the right, with counters telling you what is new for you and
what you have not yet sent to the agent.
templates.author: trisiak

choices.summary: notify presses on a document with no notify-agent frontmatter key reach no agent
choices.resolution: set notify-agent: in the document's frontmatter, or add SPEC_WORKBENCH_NOTIFY_AGENT=<agent> to the environment= line on the spec-workbench supervisord entry

choices.summary: comments and replies made through the web UI are signed 'user' by default
choices.resolution: add SPEC_WORKBENCH_AUTHOR=<name> to the environment= line on the spec-workbench supervisord entry

choices.summary: the app opens the bundled how-to-use intro (docs/specs/how_to_use_spec_workbench.md) as the default document
choices.resolution: point SPEC_WORKBENCH_DOC at your own workspace-root-relative markdown file on the spec-workbench supervisord entry to change it

templates.title: Find an apartment without 30 tabs
templates.description: Every San Francisco listing from every landlord site, filtered, scored and dropped on one map.
templates.what_it_is:
Aggregate, filter, score, and map SF rental listings from many landlord sites

Apartment Hunt turns the scattered, one-site-at-a-time grind of finding a rental
into a single ranked view. It scrapes rental listings from ~18 San Francisco
landlord and property-manager websites, merges duplicates that appear on more
than one site, throws out anything that fails your hard limits (rent, bedrooms,
bathrooms, square footage, city, pets), and scores what remains against your
soft preferences (dishwasher, in-unit laundry, more space, lower rent) and how
long it takes to get from each place to the locations you care about
("waypoints" -- work, a park, a friend's). What you open is a web page with a
map of San Francisco on one side, a numbered pin on every listing colored by
rank, and a sortable list of listing cards on the other. You can retune the
filters, preferences, and waypoints live and re-rank instantly, kick off a
fresh scrape on demand, and mark listings up as you go (hide, contacted, toured,
a star rating, free-text notes) -- all of which persists between sessions.
templates.author: gnguralnick

choices.summary: every scraper and the seed preferences target San Francisco specifically
choices.resolution: an adopter in another city must repoint the scrapers at their own market's sources and rewrite preferences.yaml; the @register scraper framework is reusable but the per-site parsers are not portable as-is

choices.summary: waypoint travel times use the Google Routes API only if GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY is set
choices.resolution: optional -- set GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY for real walk/transit times; unset, it falls back to straight-line estimates and nothing breaks

choices.summary: the shipped preferences include two generic sample SF waypoints
choices.resolution: replace 'Downtown SF' and 'Golden Gate Park' with the places the user actually cares about, via the in-app Config panel

choices.summary: the Equity Residential scraper is present but disabled (site behind a Cloudflare challenge)
choices.resolution: left unregistered on purpose; leave it, or re-enable if the site's protection is ever relaxed -- other scrapers are unaffected

templates.title: Read your email as a morning briefing
templates.description: Your unread Gmail, summarised overnight. GitHub notifications fold into one card per pull request.
templates.what_it_is:
Daily Digest turns an unread Gmail inbox into a morning briefing you can clear
in one pass. It fetches every unread message (optionally across several inboxes
at once), has Claude read each one into a category plus its actual content --
an action to take, a receipt, events, linked articles -- and renders each email
as a single card that shows all of that in place.

GitHub sends one email per
event on a pull request, so an active PR can leave a dozen unread messages;
those are folded into one card per pull request, with the PR's state, a
CI-failing badge, an AI status line, and an activity timeline. From each card
you triage the message straight back to Gmail -- keep, archive, file under a
receipts label, or trash -- and dismiss it, with a "to go" count that ends in an
all-caught-up state.

Anything worth reading later goes on a persistent reading
list, and "View original" shows the raw email HTML in a sandboxed iframe. The
whole thing is a web page served at `/service/daily-digest/`; a background loop
re-reads the inbox hourly so the digest stays current on its own, and a
per-email cache keeps those refreshes cheap.
templates.author: gnguralnick

choices.summary: the digest reads only the single default latchkey Gmail account, because the source mind's DAILY_DIGEST_ACCOUNTS inbox list is not shipped
choices.resolution: to read and merge several inboxes, set DAILY_DIGEST_ACCOUNTS to a comma-separated list of the adopter's own Gmail addresses, each connected in latchkey

choices.summary: the receipts label must already exist in Gmail for the Receipts triage action to work
choices.resolution: create the label named by DAILY_DIGEST_RECEIPTS_LABEL (default 'Receipts and invoices'), or point the var at an existing label

choices.summary: optional run tunables control how much is processed and how often the digest refreshes
choices.resolution: set DAILY_DIGEST_MAX_EMAILS (cap per run per account; 0 = no limit) and DAILY_DIGEST_REFRESH_SECONDS (background refresh cadence; default 3600) if the defaults don't fit

templates.title: Never drop a follow-up
templates.description: Tracks everyone you owe a reply, drafts it in your voice, and tells you when they opened it.
templates.what_it_is:
Orchard is a recruiter's outreach workbench: a single-page app for running
cold-outreach campaigns end to end. It solves the "I have a list of people to
reach out to, help me contact them and track what happens" problem. The user
opens one board that shows a candidate table with a three-stage pipeline (not
contacted -> reached out -> replied), a compose panel with a live email
preview, a writing-voice panel, a settings panel, and open notifications.

From that board the recruiter adds candidates, writes reusable email templates
whose `{{first_name}}` / `{{company}}` / `{{role}}` / `{{sender_name}}` tokens
are filled in per candidate, and sends the message through the Gmail API from
one of three sending inboxes (their own connected mailbox plus two teammate
aliases). Several assists are built in: Claude can draft a template in a chosen
sender's writing "voice" from pasted samples, or generate a one-line "why I'm
reaching out" from a candidate's links; ContactOut can look up a candidate's
email from their LinkedIn URL. Every sent email carries an invisible 1x1
tracking pixel served over a public Cloudflare tunnel, so the app records when
a candidate opens it and raises a notification; it also detects replies and
folds in follow-ups the recruiter sent from their own mail client, keeping each
candidate's send history complete.
templates.author: mangonomnom

templates.title: Search everything you have ever written
templates.description: Copies your Slack, email, GitHub and Notion into a private store only you and your Mind can read.
templates.what_it_is:
datalib gives a mind a private, always-local copy of the user's own data --
their Slack messages, email, GitHub activity, Notion pages, and chat history --
mirrored out of those services into a single store on the mind's disk. Once
mirrored, the mind can search it and answer questions from it ("what did I tell
Sam about the launch?", "find the invoice email from March") without going back
out to each service. Nothing leaves the mind: the data is fetched with the
user's own credentials (via latchkey) and stored locally. It is opt-in on
purpose -- concentrating this much personal data is powerful and sensitive, so a
mind only gets it when the user chooses this inspiration.
templates.author: qi-imbue

templates.title: Scribble on any app to report a bug
templates.description: Draw, type or say what is wrong, right on the screen. It arrives in your chat as one tidy card.
templates.what_it_is:
Scribble, type, or speak UI feedback directly on any app in your workspace; it routes to your chat agent as one batched, rendered card per send.

Red Scribble solves the awkwardness of describing UI problems in prose. Once an
agent turns it on for an app, a small red circle floats in that app's lower-right
corner. Click it and the page stops responding to clicks -- your input becomes
annotation instead: draw freehand over anything, double-click to drop a typed
note, or double-click-and-hold to speak one. Click again and the page is yours
back; your marks hide but are kept. Press and hold the circle for a menu that
picks which chat receives the feedback and sends what you have gathered.

One send becomes one message: every mark, plus a single screenshot, arrives in
that chat as a card of tiles you can hover for detail. The agent reads your
intent, makes the change, and closes each scribble so it disappears from your
screen. Two delivery modes tune the pace -- **batch** waits for you to press send
and lets the agent harden its work, while **live** auto-sends a couple of seconds
after each mark and primes the agent for fast, throwaway prototyping. While it
runs, all you see is the red circle and your own annotations.
templates.author: danverbraganza

choices.summary: an app only gets Red Scribble once it carries the one-line opt-in
choices.resolution: run the enable-red-scribble skill for each app you want to scribble on; the included Scribble Box is already opted in

templates.title: Turn one post into a week of posts
templates.description: A blog post or a few bullets becomes X threads and LinkedIn posts, written in your voice and queued to go out.
templates.what_it_is:
A multi-voice, multi-format generator that turns blog posts, links, or bullet points into X threads and LinkedIn posts, with a schedule queue and a cached voice-corpus mechanism.

Thread Writer solves the "we published something, now someone has to turn it
into social posts" problem. It is a small web app (a Typefully-style reader)
that takes a source -- one of your own blog posts, any trending link you paste
in, or a few bullet points you jot down -- and drafts ready-to-post social copy
from it. Every draft can be written in one of three **voices** (Normies,
Researchers, or Quotes) and one of three **formats** (a single Tweet, a Thread
of tweets, or a long-form LinkedIn post), and any voice-and-format combination
can be generated or regenerated on demand with one click. When it is running the
user opens a tab and sees two surfaces: a **reader** that renders a chosen
draft as a stack of tweet cards with live character counts, a voice dropdown, a
format tab toggle, and a Publish button; and a **Schedule** view with an "Up
next" queue of what is due to post (each with a recommended, staggered date), a
month calendar of published posts, and paste-a-link / paste-your-notes inputs.
Publishing never auto-posts -- it copies the text to the clipboard and opens X's
or LinkedIn's composer so the user reviews and sends it themselves. The voices
are not one-line style hints -- each is grounded in a large corpus of real
example writing that is sent to the model as a cached prompt prefix, so drafts
imitate a genuine register rather than a description of one.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Send a letter by carrier pigeon
templates.description: It flies at real pigeon speed and lands as an email. Sometimes the bird dies on the way.
templates.what_it_is:
Carrier-pigeon messaging: a message flies at real pigeon speed by distance, becomes a real email when the bird lands, and sometimes the bird dies in transit.

Pigeon Post is a whimsical but genuinely functional messaging toy. The user
writes a short note (a "scroll"), addresses it to a recipient's email, and picks
a launch city and a destination city. Instead of sending instantly, the app
releases a carrier pigeon that flies at real pigeon speed -- calibrated so that
Los Angeles to New York takes about 22 hours -- and the note only becomes a real
email, sent from the user's own Gmail, if and when the bird lands. Longer flights
are deadlier: each release rolls a distance-based survival chance, and sometimes
the pigeon dies mid-journey and the message is never delivered. The user sees a
chat-style conversation view for each recipient alongside a live map that draws
the great-circle route and animates the bird's current position along it; a
limited stock of fast "express" pigeons lets them watch a whole delivery play out
in seconds. It is deliberately slow, occasionally fatal, and the payoff is a real
email arriving at the other end.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Find music you have not heard yet
templates.description: A daily scout through the scenes you love and the ones you keep meaning to try. Listen and follow in one place.
templates.what_it_is:
A daily music scout: new artists in the scenes you love, are curious about, and haven't explored yet -- listen and follow in one place.

Overtone is a daily music scout. Each morning it surfaces new artists in three
modes -- DEEPER (a scene you're steeped in), BROADER (a scene you've dipped into),
and OTHER (something with no foothold in your library yet, rotated for variety).
Each candidate is checked against your entire followed-artist list so nothing you
already have resurfaces, carries a quoted line from a real review or list with a
link back to the source, and is verified so the mapped Spotify artist actually
matches the reviewed release. You open one web page, listen to recent releases
inline, and follow or skip in place -- discovery and action in one surface instead
of scattered across reviews, playlists, and the Spotify app.
templates.author: glennm292

templates.title: Review pull requests without the noise
templates.description: A cleaner window on your GitHub pull requests that knows what the code around a change does.
templates.what_it_is:
A self-hosted web app for reviewing your own GitHub pull requests with real
code context, because GitHub's own diff UI shows you changed lines but almost
none of the surrounding code they touch. It solves that: when you open a PR it
downloads the entire repository at the PR's head commit and renders each changed
file as a full-file diff in a Monaco editor, so you read a change in the context
of the whole file, not a keyhole hunk. On top of that it adds code intelligence
-- open any file in the repo, find every usage of a symbol across the whole
tree, and get hover / go-to-definition for Python and JavaScript/TypeScript
(with an opt-in "rich types" mode that resolves third-party and inferred types
too). When it is running the user opens a single tab: a list of their open pull
requests (ones they authored plus ones they were asked to review) annotated with
CI, review, and merge-conflict status, and clicking any PR drops them into the
code-aware review view. From there they can act on the PR without leaving the app
-- post comments, submit a line-comment review (approve / request changes /
comment), edit the title and description, close/reopen or merge, resolve and
reopen review-comment threads, flip a PR between draft and ready-for-review, and
even hand a question to a headless agent that investigates inside the
checked-out code.
templates.author: gnguralnick

choices.summary: Scoped to a single authenticated GitHub viewer -- the PR list is whoever latchkey's GitHub credentials resolve to, with no notion of teams or org-wide review queues.
choices.resolution: An adopter who wants a shared/team view generalizes the list query (drive it off explicit repo/org filters rather than the single viewer) and rethinks write-back attribution.

choices.summary: Rich types depends on the cached tree's package managers resolving cleanly -- repos with private registries, unusual build steps, or install scripts needing extra secrets may fail to prepare, and the app silently falls back to the zero-setup engines (tree-sitter / bare Jedi).
choices.resolution: An adopter targeting such repos preinstalls or customizes the prepare step. Note the deliberate typescript@5 pin -- newer TypeScript dropped the classic language-service API the tool relies on.

choices.summary: The internal port 8082 is hardcoded in two places -- the supervisord forward_port.py wiring and the server's PR_REVIEW_PORT default -- which must agree.
choices.resolution: An adopter who needs a different port changes both the [program:pr-review] forward_port.py --url and PR_REVIEW_PORT.

choices.summary: The GraphQL features (thread resolution, draft toggle) depend on a latchkey new enough to expose github-graphql-api (>= 2.20.2); on an older latchkey those actions error rather than hide, since the app does not yet detect this and disable the controls.
choices.resolution: An adopter on an old latchkey upgrades it, or accepts that those specific buttons error while the REST features work.

templates.title: Pitch your half-formed idea to a room
templates.description: A panel of invented experts argues over it, tears it apart, and tells you what you are missing.
templates.author: TABARC-Code

templates.title: Plan your day by dragging blocks
templates.description: Hard deadlines on a calendar, everything else dragged into the hours you actually have.
templates.what_it_is:
Lego-style todo planner: a deadline calendar of hard due dates plus drag-and-drop daily planning, with goals sections and a Google Calendar today view.

The Lego Todo Planner is a single-page personal daily planner for someone who
juggles a backlog of deadline-bearing tasks and wants to decide, each morning,
what to actually work on today. It solves the gap between "everything I owe" and
"what I'll do now": a "To do" backlog collects tasks (each with a title, an
optional hard deadline, a 0-100% progress bar, and dated freeform notes), and
the user drags the ones that matter into a "Today" column to build the day's
plan. A monthly "Deadlines" calendar marks every task's due date so nothing
sneaks up, and two freeform notes areas -- "Long Term Goals" and "Outstanding
but not immediately actionable" -- hold the thinking that isn't a task yet. The
"Today" column also stitches in the user's real Google Calendar events for the
current day, so the plan sits alongside actual meetings. A second "Saves" tab
keeps three freeform lists (Opportunities, Events, Interests). Everything the
user types persists automatically to a local JSON store, so the board is exactly
as they left it on the next visit. When it is running the user opens one web
page: a calm, paper-styled board they read, drag, and edit directly in place.
templates.author: cinxwei

templates.title: Read Twitter as an encyclopedia
templates.description: Your real timeline set as antique pages, one topic per page. You turn pages instead of scrolling forever.
templates.what_it_is:
Your real X (Twitter) home timeline rendered as an antique encyclopedia: posts grouped by topic, one topic per page -- you turn pages from topic to topic instead of scrolling an endless stream.

Dictionary Feed is a paginated reading view of your X/Twitter home timeline,
styled as a page from an antique encyclopedia. It solves the doomscroll: instead
of an infinite stream, your timeline is fetched, grouped into topics, and bound
into pages -- one topic per page. You read it by "turning pages" from one topic
to the next rather than scrolling forever. Each entry shows the post's author,
text, and engagement, and links out to the original post on X as well as to its
raw stored record. When it is running the user opens a single web page: an
encyclopedia-styled spread of the current topic's posts, with page navigation to
move between topics and a refresh action to re-gather the latest timeline.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Keep a bullet journal that fills itself
templates.description: Email, calendar and Slack become today's log of tasks, events and notes. Tick them off, track your mood.
templates.what_it_is:
A single dot-grid "rapid log" page in the bullet-journal tradition. It pulls
items from your email, calendar, and Slack and renders them as tasks, events,
and notes with the classic bullet symbols -- a dot for a task, an open circle
for an event, a dash for a note, a star for a priority. Instead of jumping
between three inboxes and a calendar, the user opens one calm analog-style page
that unifies the day: a task you can check off (and the checkmark persists), an
event with its time and attendees, a note jotted from a Slack thread. Each
entry keeps a "view original" affordance that opens the underlying record (the
rendered email, the raw event) so nothing is lost between the source and the
journal view. A small daily mood tracker sits on the page -- tap a day to cycle
its mood dot -- so the log carries a little of the reflective habit that paper
bullet journals are known for.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Make bulk senders go away
templates.description: Groups every high-volume sender so you unsubscribe, mute or archive the whole lot in one pass.
templates.what_it_is:
Email Go Away is an inbox-triage web view. It solves the "my inbox is full of
noise" problem by turning a cluttered mailbox into a single one-screen
decision. Instead of a flat list of messages, it groups your mail by sender
into two columns: a **GO AWAY** column for the bulk / newsletter / promotional
senders that dominate the inbox, and a **keep** column for the people and
accounts you actually care about. Each sender shows how many messages it has
sent and the exact action GO AWAY will take for it -- one-click unsubscribe,
plain unsubscribe, or mute + clear existing -- so you can clear out a
high-volume sender in one pass rather than deleting messages one at a time.
Every individual message keeps a "view raw / open in Gmail" affordance so you
can inspect the original email in its native rendered form before acting. When
it is running, the user opens a single page that lays out all their bulk
senders on the left, each with one GO AWAY control, and the senders worth
keeping cleanly separated on the right.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Never answer that person again
templates.description: Pick who gets an automatic polite brush-off on Slack and email. Every reply it sends is logged for you.
templates.what_it_is:
Manage a list of people whose Slack DMs and emails get an automatic non-response, and log every reply sent

Non-Responder is a "standing reply desk." Some people you simply never want to
respond to individually -- a persistent recruiter, a vendor who won't stop
following up, an ex-colleague -- but ignoring them outright feels worse than
sending something. This app lets you add those specific people (by name, Slack
@handle, Slack user, or email address); from then on, whenever any of them DMs
you on Slack or emails you, the app automatically sends ONE flat reply per
conversation ("Thanks, noted."), archives their message so it never lands in
your inbox, and logs the deflection with an excerpt of what they said, the
reply that went out, and a link back to the original message. Only people on
your list are ever touched -- everyone else reaches you exactly as before. When
it is running, the user sees a single web dashboard: the list of watched people,
the editable standing reply, per-channel on/off toggles for Slack and email, a
count of deflections this week, and a running log of every non-response sent.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: See what someone actually talks about
templates.description: Their tweets as a constellation of subjects. Click any one to read the real posts behind it.
templates.what_it_is:
An interactive topic-constellation explorer for a Twitter user's archive. It
reads a precomputed co-occurrence graph of the topics in the archive and renders
it as a force-directed constellation: each node is a topic, sized by how often it
appears and colored by the community it clusters into. Clicking any topic opens a
drawer of the real tweets that mention it -- with like and retweet counts, dates,
and "open on X" links -- and you can search topics and pan/zoom to explore the
whole map. It answers "what does this person actually talk about, and how do
those themes connect?" without making you scroll a timeline: the constellation is
the overview, and every topic is a doorway back to the source tweets. The
screenshots and demo were captured against Visakan Veerasamy's public archive
(via the Community Archive, community-archive.org) -- 267k tweets distilled into
80 topics.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Learn anything from scratch
templates.description: Ask about Roman concrete or bond yields and get a short slide deck, built on the spot, revealed one idea at a time.
templates.what_it_is:
Learn any topic from scratch as a short, progressively-revealed slide deck, generated on demand

Learn from Scratch turns any topic into a short, self-paced lesson you step through
one idea at a time. You name a topic; the agent (via the bundled `/learn-from-scratch`
skill) researches it from primary sources, proposes a brief curriculum, and — once you
approve it — writes a module of roughly 15-25 bite-sized sections. The web app renders
that module as a single screen with a vertical "detail" slider on the left: each step
down swaps in the next idea, so exactly one coherent concept is on screen at a time,
rendered with GitHub-flavored Markdown, KaTeX math, citations, and small interactive
React diagrams. A left sidebar lists every topic with search, free-form tags, and an
archive; any topic can be annotated in place or exported to PDF. Two example topics ship
with it so the app is not empty on first boot.
templates.author: NayanaBannur

templates.title: See your unread Slack as a garden
templates.description: Every unread message is a plant. The longer you leave it, the more it wilts.
templates.what_it_is:
A 3D zen-garden web view of your unread Slack messages, where each unread message is a potted plant that wilts with age.

Zenbox turns the anxiety of a cluttered Slack into something calm you actually
want to look at. Instead of a wall of red unread badges, it gives you a single
web page ("Unread Garden") that renders your unread Slack messages from the last
three days as a 3D zen garden: raked sand with a scattering of potted plants, one
plant per unread message. Fresh messages are healthy and green; as a message goes
unanswered it wilts -- yellowing after a few hours, drooping and brown after a day
-- so a glance tells you both how much is waiting and how stale it is. Hovering a
plant reveals the channel, sender, and message text; clicking opens that exact
message in Slack. The page refreshes about once a minute, and with no unreads in
the window it says "Your garden is at peace." It is a single-user, read-only
ambient view -- it never posts, marks things read, or changes anything in Slack;
it only reflects what is already there.
templates.author: pseay-imbue

templates.title: Run your week on paper you cannot lose
templates.description: Inbox, next actions, projects and a Friday review -- plain text you own, laid out like ruled paper.
templates.what_it_is:
A calm, plain-text GTD (Getting Things Done) task manager -- inbox, next actions, projects, calendar, and weekly review -- backed by markdown files and served as a ruled-paper web app.

It solves the problem of a scattered, stressful todo list by giving you a
single trusted place to capture everything and a calm workflow for deciding
what to actually do. There is no database and no cloud service: every task is
an ordinary markdown file with a little YAML header, living under
`data/.apps/gtd/items/<id>.md`, and the whole thing is served as a warm,
ruled-paper "commonplace book" web page you open as a workspace tab. A
left-hand nav clusters by mental mode -- Active (Inbox, Next Actions, Projects,
Waiting, Tickler), Holding (Someday/Maybe, Read & Review, Reference), and Time
(Today, Calendar, Weekly Review) -- each rendering the matching tasks as
editable rows. You capture by pasting a block of lines into the Inbox (one task
per line), and you process by moving items into buckets, setting due/start
dates, grouping actions under projects, and running a weekly review. The
distinctive move: the actual thinking happens in chat with an agent -- each row
has "Triage in chat", "Plan", and "Handoff" buttons that copy a ready-made
prompt to paste into your agent, and a fresh install shows a Getting Started
panel.
templates.author: pseay-imbue

templates.title: Take notes that link themselves
templates.description: Type [[like this]] to connect an idea. Pulls in Slack messages and Google Docs as things you can link to.
templates.what_it_is:
A Roam-style personal notebook for people who think by connecting ideas rather
than filing them into folders. You write in an outliner -- everything is a
nested bullet -- and you link ideas inline with `[[wiki-links]]` and reference
individual bullets with `((block references))`. Every link is bidirectional, so
each page automatically grows a **Backlinks** section (its "linked references")
showing every other place that mentions it, and a **force-directed graph** view
renders the whole web of pages and concepts so you can see clusters and bridges
at a glance. What sets it apart from a plain notes app is that outside content
is pulled in as first-class, linkable nodes: messages from **Slack** and
documents from **Google Docs** appear inline as cards you can link to like any
other note, each keeping a "view original" of the raw record and an "open in
source" jump back to the real message or doc. The result, when running, is a
single web page: a left sidebar of pages and sources, a center outliner you type
into, a backlinks panel, and a toggle to the graph -- one connected knowledge
base that spans your own notes and the conversations and docs they came from.
templates.author: jean-imbue

templates.title: Run your whole day from the keyboard
templates.description: Email, chat, calendar and tasks in one list you never touch the mouse for.
templates.what_it_is:
Unified Inbox is a single, keyboard-first web app that collapses everything
you would otherwise check across a dozen tabs -- four email accounts, Slack,
Discord, Telegram, GitHub, two calendars, a San Francisco events feed, and your
Obsidian task vault -- into one fast, read-only command center in the spirit of
Superhuman or Raycast. A background daemon pulls every source into a local JSON
cache every minute or so, so the app opens instantly to a merged, newest-first
inbox with per-source color tags and unread markers. You move with `j`/`k`,
open with `Enter`, fuzzy-search the cache with `/`, jump anywhere with `Cmd-K`,
and trigger a full-history deep search across email and Slack when a query is
active. A week / 3-day Calendar overlays Google Calendar, Zoho (CalDAV), and
Luma events (all-day items as spanning bars); a Luma SF view shows upcoming
events with full detail; a Tasks view reads open checkboxes (`- [ ]`) from an
Obsidian vault and renders an interactive force-directed graph of its
`[[wikilinks]]`; and a floating "Ask" assistant (`Cmd-J`) runs a real agent
that can read the connected accounts live to answer questions and draft
replies. It is deliberately read-and-advise only: it surfaces, summarizes, and
drafts -- it never sends mail, posts, or takes any external action.
templates.author: CarlKho-Minerva

templates.title: Build a dashboard by dragging pieces
templates.description: Drop widgets on an endless board and wire one into another. No layout to fight.
templates.what_it_is:
Widget Board is an infinite-canvas "desktop" of small, interactive widgets that
you drag around, pan/zoom across, and **wire together**: each widget exposes
output and input sockets, and you draw cables between them so a signal emitted by
one widget flows into another. It turns a set of otherwise-isolated tools into a
visual dataflow you assemble by hand -- a timer that fires a Slack message, an
email list that feeds an AI summary, a trigger button that fans out to several
receivers.

You can keep multiple named boards ("workbenches") and switch between them; each
autosaves as you work. The widget palette spans several categories: **Timers**
(countdowns and repeating intervals), **Email** (a Gmail-backed inbox reader and
a reply drafter), **Cloud storage**, **Cloud AI** (email analysis / reply
drafting), **AI Agents** (run a coding-agent task in a sandbox), **Slack** (read
channels and post messages), **IO** (printers, passthroughs, manual emitters),
**Triggers** (buttons and conditions that start a flow), and **Workbench
routing** (send/receive signals between boards). It also ships light/dark theming
with a live custom-palette editor, deep links to specific views, and full board
export/import. The entire frontend is a single self-contained `index.html` with
no build step; a small Flask backend serves it and the state / email / Slack /
agent / document APIs. When it is running, the user opens a tab and sees their
board of widgets, ready to arrange and wire.
templates.author: boweiliu

templates.title: See every unread Slack in one table
templates.description: Sender, channel, whether it is a thread, and a link straight to it. Refreshes itself every minute.
templates.what_it_is:
A live web grid of your unread Slack messages -- message, channel, sender, thread yes/no, and a direct link -- auto-refreshing every minute.

Slack buries what you have not read: unread counts are scattered across
workspaces, sidebars, and muted channels, and there is no single place to scan
everything new at a glance. This inspiration solves that with one web page -- a
grid of every unread message across the user's Slack, including muted channels
and DMs. Each row shows the message text, the channel (or DM) it came from, who
sent it, whether it belongs to a thread, and a direct "open in Slack" link back
to the original. A background job re-checks Slack every minute, so the page
stays current on its own; a small "Updated 3:41 PM" indicator in the corner
tells the user when the data last refreshed. When there is nothing unread, the
page shows a friendly "You're all caught up" state instead of an empty grid.
The user opens one tab and sees, in a single scannable list, everything waiting
for them -- and can jump straight back to any message with one click.
templates.author: pseay-imbue

templates.title: See what your agents are costing you
templates.description: Live AI spend per agent, next to CPU, memory and disk for the whole machine.
templates.what_it_is:
A host-wide monitor for Minds -- live AI cost per agent and workspace priced from transcripts, plus system activity (CPU, memory and OOM, disk, services), with cost formulas and a confidence score.

Minds Pulse is a host-wide monitor that runs as a web service in your
workspace (it opens as the `minds-pulse` tab). It answers two questions you
otherwise cannot see at a glance: "how much is the AI on this host actually
costing me, and who is spending it?" and "is this machine healthy right now?"
For cost, it reads every agent's Claude Code transcripts directly off the host,
attributes token usage to the agent and workspace that produced it, and prices
it from a mirrored copy of the mngr billing rates -- so you get live spend
broken down per agent and per workspace, with the exact cost formulas and a
confidence score shown rather than hidden. For system activity, it samples the
live machine -- CPU, memory (including the OOM shed log of processes the host
killed under memory pressure), disk usage, the supervisord service roster, and
the running agents -- refreshed on each request with a short rolling history.
The user sees a single dashboard: a vitals strip across the top and tabbed
panels (Cost, Memory, Compute, Storage, Services), styled in native Minds
colors with a "pulse" identity and a provisional build-vs-run spend projection.
It makes no external or LLM calls of its own; everything comes from reading
local host files and sampling the process table.
templates.author: MRTIBBETS

templates.title: Keep every to-do in one list
templates.description: Pulls what you promised out of Slack, Gmail and Granola, ranked, deduped, each one linked back to where you said it.
templates.what_it_is:
A unified task inbox that pulls your open to-dos from Slack, Gmail, and Granola into one ranked, deduped, source-linked list with due dates, urgency, categories, notes, and side-lists.

Your open to-dos are scattered across Slack, email, and meeting notes, and it is
easy to lose track of what actually needs doing. Task Inbox solves that by
pulling all of it into one place. It reaches into your Slack (DMs, @-mentions,
and a configured set of channels), your Gmail inbox, and your Granola meeting
notes, decides which messages are genuine to-dos, and extracts a clean task from
each one with a plain-English description, a type/category, who is asking, a due
date, and an urgency level. It then presents everything as a single web board:
open tasks grouped by due date, type, and urgency, with each task linked back to
the original Slack message or email so you can always see the source. On top of
the auto-collected tasks you can add your own, keep side-lists, attach notes,
archive items, define custom categories and filters, and restyle the board's
theme. A background scheduler refreshes the list a few times a day, so it stays
current on its own. When it is running the user opens a tab and sees their live,
ranked task list; before any accounts are connected the board simply renders
empty.
templates.author: annao-h

templates.title: Read Slack and email in one place
templates.description: One list for both, and a single box to reply from. You stop switching tabs to answer people.
templates.what_it_is:
Megabox collapses two separate message streams -- the user's real Slack and
their Gmail -- into a single place to triage and a single place to write back,
so they can clear both from one screen instead of bouncing between apps. It
ships as two web pages the user opens as workspace tabs.

The first is a **unified inbox**: an email-client-style page (a dark left rail
of filters, a middle message list, a reading pane) that merges Slack channels
and DMs -- with true unread counts, threads, quick emoji reactions, and inline
images/attachments -- together with recent Gmail collapsed by conversation,
into one queue. From it the user triages (marking a message read writes the
change back to the real Slack/Gmail; "Keep" bookmarks it locally), opens the
untouched original ("View raw", "Open in Slack", "Open in Gmail"), and hits
Reply, which hands a prefilled draft to the second page.

The second is a **channel-agnostic composer**: one interchangeable "To" field
that autocompletes across real Slack channels/users and Gmail contacts, a Send
button that morphs to show the resolved destination (a Slack channel or an
email address), browser-persisted drafts, and threaded replies. Sending is
real -- it posts to Slack and sends Gmail for the user's own account. When it
is running the user sees a "Megabox -- Unified Inbox" tab and a composer tab,
both showing their own live messages.
templates.author: pseay-imbue

templates.title: Watch the sea for a minute
templates.description: A full-screen dusk seascape, and a new quote every five minutes.
templates.what_it_is:
Calm Waves is a single-page ambient web view -- a moment of quiet you can open
in a browser tab. It solves nothing "productive"; its job is to give the user a
calm, screensaver-like place to rest their eyes. When it is running, the user
opens `/service/calm-waves/` and sees a full-screen dusk seascape: a
twilight-blue sky gradient melting into a soft rose horizon with a warm radial
glow, and three layers of smooth, sine-generated waves that drift sideways and
bob gently up and down (tuned so the layers never cross and always cover the
bottom edge). Centered above the water, an inspirational quote in a light serif
cross-fades to a new one every 5 minutes. The quotes are shuffled fresh on each
load, and clicking the quote advances to the next one early and resets the
timer. It respects the OS "reduce motion" setting by holding the animation
still. There is no dashboard, no data to manage, and nothing to log into -- the
only thing it produces is the page itself.
templates.author: pseay-imbue

shelves.title: Just for the fun of it
